Nahor
nā'hŏr
n. (grandfather and brother of Abraham — the man who stayed in Mesopotamia, and whose city and daughters supplied the wives of the covenant line)
From Hebrew Nachor, probably from nachar, to snort or breathe hard, or from a root meaning to be scorched. Two men bear it: Terah's father and Terah's son, so Abraham had both a grandfather and a brother called Nahor.

Biblical Definition

Nahor is Abraham's brother, and he is the man who did not go. When the LORD said “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house” (Gen 12:1), the family divided: Abram went, and Nahor stayed in Mesopotamia, where his household prospered and became a place on the map — the servant of Abraham “went to Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor” (Gen 24:10) to fetch a wife for Isaac, and found Rebekah at the well, granddaughter of Nahor by Milcah (Gen 11:29; Gen 22:20). A generation later Jacob went the same road for Rachel and Leah. So the wives of the patriarchs came from the branch that stayed behind, which kept the line clear of Canaan but did not keep it clear of idols: Rachel stole her father's teraphim, and when Jacob and Laban made their covenant at Mizpah, Laban swore by a plural — “The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge betwixt us” (Gen 31:53) — and Jacob pointedly sware by the fear of his father Isaac instead. Joshua puts the matter beyond doubt at Shechem: Terah, “the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor… served other gods” (Jos 24:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Nahor; in sacred history it names the grandfather of Abraham and also Abraham's brother, who dwelt in Mesopotamia.

expand to see more

NAHOR, n. The son of Serug and father of Terah, and so the grandfather of Abraham.

Also, the son of Terah and brother of Abraham and Haran.

He married Milcah, the daughter of his brother Haran, and had eight sons by her.

Bethuel his son was the father of Rebekah and of Laban.

The city of Nahor in Mesopotamia was the place whither Abraham's servant went to seek a wife for Isaac.

Key Scripture

Gen 11:29 — "And Abram and Nahor took them wives: the name of Abram's wife was Sarai; and the name of Nahor's wife, Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah, and the father of Iscah."

Gen 22:20 — "And it came to pass after these things, that it was told Abraham, saying, Behold, Milcah, she hath also born children unto thy brother Nahor;"

Gen 24:10 — "And the servant took ten camels of the camels of his master, and departed; for all the goods of his master were in his hand: and he arose, and went to Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor."

Gen 31:53 — "The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge betwixt us. And Jacob sware by the fear of his father Isaac."

Modern Corruption

Gen 31:53 is used to argue that the patriarchs were henotheists with tribal deities; Jacob's deliberate refusal of Laban's formula, and Joshua's testimony about Terah, show the text knows exactly what it is reporting.

expand to see more

Critical treatments read Laban's oath — the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor judge between us — as evidence that Israel's religion evolved out of clan deities, one god per family, and only later became monotheism. The text itself defeats the reading, because it makes a point of Jacob's refusal to say it. Laban swears by a plural; Jacob swears by “the fear of his father Isaac”, singular and personal, declining to place Nahor's gods alongside his own. And Joshua tells Israel to their face what their ancestry was: on the other side of the flood, Terah served other gods. Scripture's account of its own origin is not that Abraham's family was pure and became more so; it is that God called one idolater out of an idolatrous house, which is what grace always does.

The second thing here is Nahor as the road not taken. He stayed where the family already was, and by every visible measure he did well: a city with his name on it, eight sons by Milcah, a prosperous house at Haran that could send caravans and marry daughters into wealth. Abraham lived in tents his whole life and owned one field with a cave in it. Hebrews explains the difference and it is not a difference of temperament: he “looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10). Both brothers ended with a city. Only one of them was looking for the right one.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Nachor (H5152), Nahor; Milkah (H4435), Milcah, queen; pachad Yitschaq, the fear of Isaac; terap̄im (H8655), household gods.

expand to see more

Hebrew Nachor (H5152) — Nahor; borne by Abraham's grandfather and by his brother.

Hebrew Milkah (H4435) — Milcah, “queen”; Nahor's wife and Rebekah's grandmother.

Hebrew Bethu'el (H1328) — Bethuel, their son, father of Rebekah and Laban.

Hebrew pachad (H6343) — dread, fear; “the fear of his father Isaac”, a divine title Jacob uses twice.

Hebrew 'Aram Naharayim — Mesopotamia, Aram of the two rivers; the country of the city of Nahor.

Usage

"“Abram and Nahor took them wives” — two brothers, two roads."

"“Unto the city of Nahor” — where the covenant line went for its brides."

"“The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor” — a formula Jacob would not repeat."
